title: Hyperlambda (Magic) vs FastAPI, pooled SQLite read of ten rows
claim: On a pooled SQLite read of 10 rows at 128 connections, Hyperlambda served 3.7 times the requests per second of FastAPI on four worker processes (14 times FastAPI on one worker). Per CPU core the gap is 1.8 times, because Hyperlambda used about twice the cores. The headline needs SQLite connection pooling, which is not Magic's shipped default.

conditions.workload: GET returning the first 10 rows of the Chinook Artist table ordered by ArtistId, identical JSON verified on every server before measuring
conditions.database: Chinook SQLite, Artist table with 275 rows and 5,658 name characters, pooled connections on both sides
conditions.load_generator: wrk 4.2.0, 4 threads, 128 connections, 3 s warm-up discarded, 10 s measured, run on the same machine as the servers
conditions.machine: MacBook Pro Mac15,6, Apple M3 Pro, 11 cores, 18 GB RAM, macOS 14.8
conditions.python: 3.13.9, fastapi 0.161.1, uvicorn 0.54.0, aiosqlite 0.22.1, uvloop 0.23.0, httptools 0.9.0, async handlers, no ORM, no middleware

limits: One machine, one 10-row read, localhost, no authentication, no writes or joins.
Hyperlambda used about twice the cores of four-worker FastAPI, so 3.7 times is a whole-machine figure and 1.8 times is the per-core figure.
With Magic's shipped Pooling=False the same read does 4,232 requests per second, which is slower than four-worker FastAPI with per-request connections (6,245).
On a trivial string-concatenation endpoint FastAPI is more efficient per core.

Four FastAPI workers was the best Python configuration found. More workers were slower: 11 workers did 10,778 requests per second at 128 connections. Runs with 6, 8 and 10 workers also gave lower throughput but were not recorded, so only 1, 4 and 11 are published. Why more workers are slower was not investigated.
Measured mostly by Claude, an AI model, under the supervision of Magic's author, who wrote Magic. No independent replication has been published.
reproduce: The article contains setup.sh, bench.py, app.py, requirements.txt and the three Hyperlambda endpoints in full. About 20 minutes, needing git, the .NET 10 SDK, Python 3.13, sqlite3, rsync, curl and wrk.
